# Military intelligence and codebreaking (`military_intelligence_codebreaking`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by cryptography, probability_statistics, electromagnetic_waves_radio, programmable_computer
- Core idea: Decisions should rest on organised knowledge of the enemy: scouts, prisoners, deserters, merchants, paid agents and intercepted letters, collected by a permanent office, compared with each other and reported honestly to the commander. Simple substitution ciphers are broken by counting letter frequencies, so any long message in such a cipher must be assumed read. One's own messages need a better cipher and frequent changes of key. A broken enemy cipher is worth more than an army only while the enemy does not know, so the results must be used sparingly and with a cover story.
- Pitfalls:
  - Telling the ruler what he wants to hear; most intelligence failures are failures of judgement, not of collection
  - Acting on decrypts so openly that the enemy changes his cipher
  - Trusting one's own cipher because it looks complicated (German confidence in Enigma)
  - Crediting Turing alone with Enigma; Polish mathematicians first broke it in 1932 and handed over their methods in 1939
  - A single agent's report is a rumour until confirmed from an independent source
- History: china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – Sun Tzu, chapter 13, five kinds of spies; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra describes a state network of stationary and roving agents; greece: 5th c. BC – Spartan scytale (whether it was a cipher device is disputed); rome: 1st c. BC – Caesar's shift cipher (Suetonius, Julius 56) and his systematic use of scouts and exploratores; islamic: 9th c. – al-Kindi describes frequency analysis; 1683 – both sides at Vienna use couriers and spies through the lines (the messenger Kolschitzky); europe: c. 1467 – Alberti's cipher disc; 1506 – Venice appoints Giovanni Soro cipher secretary; 17th–18th c. – black chambers in Paris, London and Vienna; 1917 – Zimmermann telegram; 1932 – Rejewski breaks Enigma; 1939–1945 – Bletchley Park; americas: 1940 – US breaks the Japanese Purple cipher; 1942 – naval decrypts help the US fleet anticipate the Japanese attack at Midway
- Read:
  - David Kahn, The Codebreakers (1967)
  - Christopher Andrew, The Secret World: A History of Intelligence (2018)
  - Sun Tzu, The Art of War, chapter 13 (tr. Samuel B. Griffith, 1963)
